successor: British East India Company (through client nawab Mir Jafar)
notes: Plassey, 23 June 1757: East India Company army (external to nawabi apparatus) defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah; Clive installed Mir Jafar as client nawab; Company dominance followed (diwani 1765, nawab pensioned 1793). Q4: Alivardi's 1740 usurpation at Giria, Maratha raids.

successor: Hawaii III (Hawaii Island polity under Umi-a-Liloa and his line)
source1: Patrick V. Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings: Divine Kingship and the Rise of Archaic States in Ancient Hawai'i, University of California Press 2010 - https://www.ucpress.edu/books/how-chiefs-became-kings/paper
notes: Boundary c.1580 likely marks consolidation of Hawaii Island under the ruling Pili line (Umi-a-Liloa displaced half-brother Hakau, then subdued district chiefs): internal, ruling line continued. Umi's dating varies (c.1490-1600); thin sources.

successor: Achaemenid Empire (Sogdiana); settlement continued at Afrasiab/Samarkand
source1: E. de La Vaissiere, 'Sogdiana iii. History and Archeology', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/sogdiana-iii-history-and-archeology
source2: E. V. Rtveladze and G. A. Pugachenkova, 'Afrasiab ii. The ruined site', Encyclopaedia Iranica I/6, 1984 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/afrasiab-the-ruined-site
notes: Archaeological phase, no recorded central authority. Cyrus II conquered Sogdiana c.540 BCE (documented, but S4 excludes T2); Afrasiab/Marakanda settled 7th-6th c. BCE and occupied continuously while Koktepe declined: settlement continuity.

Varmans ruled Vanga from Vikramapura; Vijayasena of the Radha-based Senas (outside Varman realm) issued Barrackpur grant from Vikramapura, implying he ousted the Varmans mid-12th c. after Bhojavarman. Listed Deva dynasty came later.

source2: US National Park Service, 'History & Culture', Pu'ukohola Heiau National Historic Site - https://www.nps.gov/puhe/learn/historyculture/index.htm
notes: 1778 is Cook's arrival, not a political break: Kalaniopuu ruled Hawaii Island until 1782; insider succession war (1782-91) won by his nephew Kamehameha, who kept and expanded the polity. Q4: Kalaniopuu's c.1754 war against Alapai's heir.

source2: Britannica Editors, 'Barid Shahi dynasty', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Barid-Shahi-dynasty
notes: Sultanate dissolved 1490-1518 as provincial governors broke away (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Berar, Golconda); at capital Bidar real power passed to Barid ministers ruling via puppet Bahmanis until Barid sultanate (1531/1542). Listed Nayak successors wrong.

source2: Marsha Hill and James P. Allen, 'Egypt in the Third Intermediate Period (1070-664 B.C.)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art 2004 (rev. 2018) - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/tipd/hd_tipd.htm
notes: Libyan-era Egypt fragmented among rival dynasts; Napata-based Piye invaded c.728 BCE, took Memphis and received submission of Delta rulers; Shabaka later removed Saite Bakenrenef, completing 25th Dynasty rule. Database 747 is Piye's accession.

successor: Monte Alban IIIB-IV (same Zapotec state at Monte Alban)
source2: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Historic Centre of Oaxaca and Archaeological Site of Monte Alban' - https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/415/
notes: 500 CE is a ceramic-phase boundary (IIIA to IIIB): Monte Alban remained the Zapotec capital, flourishing to c.800-850 CE, so central authority continued. No documented crisis around 500.

successor: Republic of China (Nationalist government) continuing to 1949; then People's Republic of China
source2: Britannica Editors, 'Chinese Civil War', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/event/Chinese-Civil-War
notes: Entity with Nanjing capital = Republic of China; Nationalist government ruled mainland 1928-1949, so database end 1941 is not a political break. Mainland rule ended 1949 with Communist civil-war victory (PRC). Database dates look arbitrary.

successor: Neo-Assyrian Empire (vassal kings from c.732 BCE; province 713 BCE)
source1: Dominique Collon, 'Anatolia: The neo-Hittite states from c.1180 to 700 BCE', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/Anatolia/The-neo-Hittite-states-from-c-1180-to-700-bce
source2: Britannica Editors, 'Tabal', Encyclopaedia Britannica (summary of the same article; no independent second source could be opened) - https://www.britannica.com/place/Tabal
notes: Assyria made Tabal tributary (738), deposed Wasusarma c.732 installing Hulli, then Sargon II deported Ambaris and ended Tabal as a separate state (713). Tuwana (Tyana) stayed an Assyrian vassal. Database 730 = Wasusarma's deposition.
